Here we want to evaluate the consequence of low TCR read-depth. For example, since many samples only have a few TCRs, would it be helpful to exlude those samples. The conclusion is "no", there is no advantage to do so. 

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

# Setup

## Parameters
```{r}
chain = params$chain

cat("chain:", chain, "\n")

stopifnot(chain == "alpha")
```


## R library and data input

```{r}
library(data.table)

library(viridis)

theme_set(theme_classic())
data_dir = "~/research/data/TCR/TCGA/_processed_data"
```


# Load data

## Read in data

These TCR data have already been aggregated at participant level and a TCR is defined by the aaSeq.  
```{r}
TCR_data   = fread(file.path(data_dir, sprintf("TCR_%s_5.tsv", chain)))
mut_data   = fread(file.path(data_dir, "mutation_freq_geq_5.tsv"))
sample_info = fread(file.path(data_dir, "sample_info_intersection.tsv"))

dim(TCR_data)
dim(mut_data)
dim(sample_info)

head(TCR_data)
head(mut_data)
head(sample_info)

participants = sample_info$participant

TCR_mat = get_TCR_matrix(TCR_data, participants, dichotomize = FALSE)
mut_mat = get_mut_matrix(mut_data, participants)

stopifnot(setequal(participants, colnames(TCR_mat)))
stopifnot(setequal(participants, colnames(mut_mat)))

TCR_mat = TCR_mat[,match(participants, colnames(TCR_mat))]
mut_mat = mut_mat[,match(participants, colnames(mut_mat))]

dim(TCR_mat)
TCR_mat[1:2,1:3]

dim(mut_mat)
mut_mat[1:2,1:3]

TCR_rd  = sample_info$abundance
TCR_rd2 = colSums(TCR_mat)
summary(TCR_rd)
summary(TCR_rd2)

table(TCR_rd > 10)
summary(TCR_rd2[TCR_rd <= 10])
stopifnot(all(TCR_rd >= TCR_rd2))
```

## Check the distribution of TCRs

Some negative binomial regression fail, and thus we use tryCatch here.

```{r fig.width=6, fig.height=9, warning = FALSE}
tb1 = table(c(TCR_mat))
tb1
(tb1)/sum(tb1)

pars = matrix(NA, nrow=nrow(TCR_mat), ncol=5)

for(i in 1:nrow(TCR_mat)){
  if(i %% 200 == 0) {cat (i, date(), "\n")}
  yi = TCR_mat[i,]

  gi1 <- tryCatch({
    gi1 = glm.nb(yi ~ log10(TCR_rd + 0.5))
    gi1
    }, error = function(e) {NULL})
  
  if(is.null(gi1)){ next }
  
  gi0 = glm.nb(yi ~ 1)
  ai  = anova(gi0, gi1)
  
  pars[i,1:2] = as.numeric(gi1$coefficients)
  pars[i,3] = gi1$theta
  pars[i,4] = gi1$SE.theta
  pars[i,5] = ai$`Pr(Chi)`[2]
}

colnames(pars) = c("b0", "b1", "theta", "theta_SE", "pval")
dim(pars)
pars[1:2,]

pars = as.data.frame(pars)

glist = list()

for(k in 1:ncol(pars)){
  var_k = names(pars)[k]
    
  if(var_k == "theta" || var_k == "theta_SE"){
    gk = ggplot(pars, aes(x = log10(.data[[var_k]]))) + 
      geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "lightblue", color = "darkblue")
  }else{
    gk = ggplot(pars, aes(x = .data[[var_k]])) + 
      geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "lightblue", color = "darkblue")
  }
  glist[[k]] = gk
}

glist[[6]] = ggplot(pars, aes(x = -log10(pval))) +  
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "lightblue", color = "darkblue")


ggarrange(plotlist = glist, nrow=3, ncol=2)

```

## Scatter plot of nb regression results

By the definition used in glm.nb, variance = $\mu + \mu^2/\theta$, threfore large theta means closer to a Poisson distribution. 

```{r fig.width=6, fig.height=9}
pars$prop2 = rowMeans(TCR_mat > 1)

glist2 = list()
glist2[[1]] = ggplot(data = pars, mapping = aes(x = log10(theta), y = log10(theta_SE))) +
  geom_point(aes(alpha = 0.5)) + theme(legend.position = "none")

glist2[[2]] = ggplot(data = pars, mapping = aes(x = prop2, y = log10(theta))) +
  geom_point(aes(alpha = 0.5)) + theme(legend.position = "none")

glist2[[3]] = ggplot(data = pars, mapping = aes(x = b0, y = log10(theta))) +
  geom_point(aes(alpha = 0.5)) + theme(legend.position = "none")

glist2[[4]] = ggplot(data = pars, mapping = aes(x = b0, y = b1)) +
  geom_point(aes(alpha = 0.5)) + theme(legend.position = "none")

glist2[[5]] = ggplot(data = pars, mapping = aes(x = b1, y = -log10(pval))) +
  geom_point(aes(alpha = 0.5)) + theme(legend.position = "none")

glist2[[6]] = ggplot(data = pars, mapping = aes(x = -log10(pval), y = log10(theta))) +
  geom_point(aes(alpha = 0.5)) + theme(legend.position = "none")

ggarrange(plotlist = glist2, nrow=3, ncol=2)

```

## Check a few TCRs with very large or very small theta

Note that large theta means smaller variance. It seems the theta is small if there are non-zero counts for smaller TCR depth

```{r fig.width=6, fig.height=9}
w_large_theta = which(pars$prop2 > 0 & pars$theta > 100)
w_small_theta = which(pars$prop2 > 0 & pars$theta < 0.01)

length(w_large_theta)
length(w_small_theta)

glist_large = glist_small = list()

for(i in 1:6){
  y_large = TCR_mat[w_large_theta[i],]
  y_small = TCR_mat[w_small_theta[i],]
  
  df1 = data.frame(TCR_rd, y_large_theta = y_large, y_small_theta = y_small)
  
  glist_large[[i]] = ggplot(data = df1, 
                            aes(x = log10(TCR_rd + 0.5), y = y_large_theta)) + 
    geom_pointdensity() + scale_color_viridis() + theme(legend.position = "none")
  
  glist_small[[i]] = ggplot(data = df1, 
                            aes(x = log10(TCR_rd + 0.5), y = y_small_theta)) + 
    geom_pointdensity() + scale_color_viridis() + theme(legend.position = "none")
}

ggarrange(plotlist = glist_large, nrow=3, ncol=2)
ggarrange(plotlist = glist_small, nrow=3, ncol=2)

```

## Check a few TCRs with large or small slope

There is a strong negative association between b0 and b1. The mean value (reflected by b0) is larger if there are more non-zero counts. When there are more non-zero counts, they are likely observed at lower read-depth, and thus smaller slope b1? That make sense, but it is not clear why the relation between b0 and b1 is stron linear. 

```{r fig.width=6, fig.height=9}
quantile(pars$b1, probs = c(0.01, 0.05, 0.95, 0.99), na.rm = TRUE)

w_large_b1 = which(pars$prop2 > 0 & pars$b1 > 4)
w_small_b1 = which(pars$prop2 > 0 & pars$b1 < 0.8)

length(w_large_b1)
length(w_small_b1)

glist_large = glist_small = list()

for(i in 1:6){
  y_large = TCR_mat[w_large_b1[i],]
  y_small = TCR_mat[w_small_b1[i],]
  
  df1 = data.frame(TCR_rd, y_large_b1 = y_large, y_small_b1 = y_small)
  
  glist_large[[i]] = ggplot(data = df1, 
                            aes(x = log10(TCR_rd + 0.5), y = y_large_b1)) + 
    geom_pointdensity() + scale_color_viridis() + theme(legend.position = "none")
  
  glist_small[[i]] = ggplot(data = df1, 
                            aes(x = log10(TCR_rd + 0.5), y = y_small_b1)) + 
    geom_pointdensity() + scale_color_viridis() + theme(legend.position = "none")
}

ggarrange(plotlist = glist_large, nrow=3, ncol=2)
ggarrange(plotlist = glist_small, nrow=3, ncol=2)

```


## Simulate TCR data

Use the results from the following a few examples to guide the simulation.

Results when we restrict the samples with TCR read-depth larger than 10. Note that we only consider alpha chain here.

```
CAGTSGTYKYIF	BRAF:7:140453136:A:T	0.0009
CAVRGTYKYIF      TP53:17:7578442:T:C 4.304067e-06
CAVRGNDYKLSF   PIK3CA:3:178952090:G:C 5.545693e-06
```

When we use all the samples

```
CAVRGTYKYIF      TP53:17:7578442:T:C 1.375570e-06
```

### Check the association strength between somatic mutation and TCR

For simplicity, here we only consider alpha chain

```{r fig.width=6, fig.height=3, warning = FALSE}
par1 = apply(pars, 2, median, na.rm = TRUE)
par1
dim(TCR_mat)
TCR_mat[1:2,1:3]

dim(mut_mat)
mut_mat[1:2,1:3]

n_mut = rowSums(mut_mat)
summary(n_mut)
sort(n_mut, decreasing = TRUE)[1:10]

# repeat BRAF mutation here since it corresponds to two TCRs

mut2check = c("BRAF:7:140453136:A:T", 
              "TP53:17:7578442:T:C", "PIK3CA:3:178952090:G:C")

x_mat = mut_mat[match(mut2check, rownames(mut_mat)),]
dim(x_mat)
x_mat[1:2,1:4]
rowSums(x_mat)

# Just check three TCRs here
TCR2check = c("CAGTSGTYKYIF", "CAVRGTYKYIF", "CAVRGNDYKLSF")

y_mat = TCR_mat[match(TCR2check, rownames(TCR_mat)),]
dim(y_mat)
y_mat[,1:4]
rowSums(y_mat)

df_res = data.frame(mutation = mut2check[1:3], TCR = TCR2check[1:3], 
                    pval=NA, pval_subset=NA, b1=NA, b1_subset=NA)

for(k in 1:3){
  y_k = y_mat[k,]
  x_k = x_mat[k,]
  
  df_k = data.frame(y=y_k, x=as.factor(x_k), rd = TCR_rd)

  gk  = glm.nb(y ~ log10(rd + 0.5) + x, data=df_k)
  gk0 = glm.nb(y ~ log10(rd + 0.5), data=df_k)
  ak  = anova(gk, gk0)
  df_res$pval[k] = ak$`Pr(Chi)`[2]
  df_res$b1[k] = coef(gk)[["x1"]]

  df_k_sub = df_k[df_k$rd > 10,]
  gk  = glm.nb(y ~ log10(rd + 0.5) + x, data=df_k_sub)
  gk0 = glm.nb(y ~ log10(rd + 0.5), data=df_k_sub)
  ak  = anova(gk, gk0)
  df_res$pval_subset[k] = ak$`Pr(Chi)`[2]
  df_res$b1_subset[k] = coef(gk)[["x1"]]

  gp_k = ggplot(data = df_k, aes(x=log10(rd + 0.5), y=y)) + 
    geom_pointdensity() + scale_color_viridis() + 
    geom_vline(xintercept = log10(10.5)) + 
    theme(legend.position = "none") + 
    ggtitle(paste(mut2check[k], TCR2check[k])) + 
    facet_wrap(~ x) 
  print(gp_k)
}

df_res
```

### Simulate data for less frequent mutation of BRAF:7:140453136:A:T

```{r fig.width=3, fig.height=3, warning=FALSE}
x = x_mat[1,]
sum(x)

mu = par1["b0"] + par1["b1"]*log10(TCR_rd + 0.5) + 2.4*x
par(bty = "n")
plot(log10(TCR_rd + 0.5), mu)

set.seed(39)

stopifnot(length(mu) == ncol(TCR_mat))
y_simu = rnbinom(n=ncol(TCR_mat), mu=exp(mu), size=par1["theta"])
par(bty = "n")
plot(mu, y_simu)

set.seed(39)

rd_cutoff = 10
table(TCR_rd > rd_cutoff)

n_simu = 200
pval_df = data.frame(p_all = rep(NA, n_simu), p_subset = rep(NA, n_simu))

for(i in 1:n_simu){
  y_simu = rnbinom(n=ncol(TCR_mat), mu=exp(mu), size=par1["theta"])
  y_all  = as.numeric(y_simu > 0)
  df_i   = data.frame(y = y_all, x = x, rd = TCR_rd)
  
  l0 = glm(y ~ rd, family = "binomial", data = df_i)
  l1 = glm(y ~ x * rd, family = "binomial", data = df_i)
  lrt = anova(l0, l1, test = "LRT")
  pval_df$p_all[i] = lrt$`Pr(>Chi)`[2]
  
  df_i_subset = df_i[df_i$rd > rd_cutoff,]
  l0 = glm(y ~ rd, family = "binomial", data = df_i_subset)
  l1 = glm(y ~ x * rd, family = "binomial", data = df_i_subset)
  lrt = anova(l0, l1, test = "LRT")

  pval_df$p_subset[i] = lrt$`Pr(>Chi)`[2]
}

ggplot(pval_df, aes(x = p_all)) + 
      geom_histogram(breaks = seq(0,1,by=0.02), fill = "lightblue", color = "darkblue")

ggplot(pval_df, aes(x = p_subset)) + 
      geom_histogram(breaks = seq(0,1,by=0.02), fill = "lightblue", color = "darkblue")

ggplot(pval_df, aes(x = -log10(p_all), y = -log10(p_subset))) + 
      geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0)

```

### Simulate data for less frequent mutation of PIK3CA:3:178952090:G:C

```{r fig.width=3, fig.height=3, warning=FALSE}
x = x_mat[3,]
sum(x)
mu = par1["b0"] + par1["b1"]*log10(TCR_rd + 0.5) + 5.4*x
par(bty = "n")
plot(log10(TCR_rd + 0.5), mu)

set.seed(39)

stopifnot(length(mu) == ncol(TCR_mat))
y_simu = rnbinom(n=ncol(TCR_mat), mu=exp(mu), size=par1["theta"])
par(bty = "n")
plot(mu, y_simu)

set.seed(39)

rd_cutoff = 10
table(TCR_rd > rd_cutoff)

n_simu = 200
pval_df = data.frame(p_all = rep(NA, n_simu), p_subset = rep(NA, n_simu))

for(i in 1:n_simu){
  y_simu = rnbinom(n=ncol(TCR_mat), mu=exp(mu), size=par1["theta"])
  y_all  = as.numeric(y_simu > 0)

  l0 = glm(y ~ rd, family = "binomial", data = df_i)
  l1 = glm(y ~ x * rd, family = "binomial", data = df_i)
  lrt = anova(l0, l1, test = "LRT")
  pval_df$p_all[i] = lrt$`Pr(>Chi)`[2]
  
  df_i_subset = df_i[df_i$rd > rd_cutoff,]
  l0 = glm(y ~ rd, family = "binomial", data = df_i_subset)
  l1 = glm(y ~ x * rd, family = "binomial", data = df_i_subset)
  lrt = anova(l0, l1, test = "LRT")

  pval_df$p_subset[i] = lrt$`Pr(>Chi)`[2]
}

ggplot(pval_df, aes(x = p_all)) + 
      geom_histogram(breaks = seq(0,1,by=0.02), fill = "lightblue", color = "darkblue")

ggplot(pval_df, aes(x = p_subset)) + 
      geom_histogram(breaks = seq(0,1,by=0.02), fill = "lightblue", color = "darkblue")

ggplot(pval_df, aes(x = -log10(p_all), y = -log10(p_subset))) +
```
